planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring after frost danger; Jelly (also sold as Mary Lane Seedless) is self-fertile and needs no pollinator, producing a long-necked, pale yellow fruit with nearly seedless amber flesh.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Jelly, marketed by some Gulf South nurseries as Mary Lane Seedless, produces a distinctive elongated, bottleneck-shaped fruit with thin yellow skin and clear amber flesh that is nearly free of viable seeds. The lack of seeds and high sugar content make it especially prized for fig preserves and jam, while the tender, sweet flesh is also excellent fresh. It ripens on a single main crop in late July into August and is grown as a cold-tolerant landscape and container fig further north than many named cultivars. As with other closed-eye types, its tight ostiole offers some resistance to the rain-driven souring that plagues open-eyed figs during humid Gulf Coast summers.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center — Figs factsheet
University of Florida IFAS Extension — The Fig (HS27/MG214)

planting.note: Plant rooted vines in late winter to early spring on a strong arbor or trellis; Dulcet is a female-flowered black muscadine and must be planted within about 25 feet of a self-fertile variety such as Cowart or Carlos to set fruit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun on a sturdy overhead arbor or high-wire trellis; Dulcet is one of the black-fruited selections to emerge from the University of Georgia's early twentieth-century muscadine breeding program, prized for generations of Southern growers for its rich, sweet flavor and productive vigor. Because it carries only female flowers, it produces no pollen of its own and needs a nearby self-fertile black or bronze cultivar to ensure a full fruit set every season. Like other muscadines, it shrugs off Pierce's disease, black rot, and the humid-summer fungal pressure that limits bunch grapes in the Gulf South, and it needs no fungicide spray program in most home gardens. Prune hard each winter back to short spurs on permanent cordons to keep the vigorous vine productive and manageable.
sources: University of Georgia College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences — Muscadine Grape Breeding Program cultivar records
Mississippi State University Extension — Establishment and Production of Muscadine Grapes (P2290)

planting.note: Plant rooted vines in late winter to early spring in full sun on a strong arbor or trellis; Golden Isles is self-fertile and ripens midseason with thin-skinned, pink-bronze berries notably milder and less musky than most muscadines.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy overhead arbor or high-wire trellis; Golden Isles was released in 1987 by University of Georgia grape breeder Ron Lane from a cross of Fry with a Creek-derived selection, and was specifically chosen for juice and wine use because its thin-skinned, pink-bronze berries have a much softer, less 'foxy' muscadine aroma than standard cultivars, making it approachable for people new to muscadine flavor. Self-fertile, it sets a reliable crop on its own and needs no companion pollinator vine. It carries the same strong native resistance to Pierce's disease and humid-climate fungal pressure that makes muscadines nearly maintenance-free in Gulf Coast gardens. Prune heavily each winter, leaving only short renewal spurs along permanent cordons, and thin dense clusters in early summer to improve airflow and fruit quality.
sources: University of Georgia Muscadine Grape Breeding Program — Golden Isles cultivar profile
University of Florida IFAS Extension — The Muscadine Grape (HS763/HS100)

planting.note: Plant rooted vines in late winter to early spring on a strong arbor or trellis; Loomis is a female-flowered black muscadine and needs a self-fertile pollinator variety such as Nesbitt or Cowart planted nearby to fruit well.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy overhead arbor or high-wire trellis; Loomis, named for the USDA breeder who developed it, produces medium-large clusters of glossy black berries with unusually high sugar content (near 20 Brix) and rich, sweet flavor that place it among the best-tasting of the black muscadines. The vine is notably vigorous with disease-resistant foliage and ripens late in the season, extending the black muscadine harvest after earlier cultivars like Cowart and Ison have finished. Because Loomis carries only female flowers, it produces no fruit on its own and must be planted within pollination range of a self-fertile variety. Prune hard each winter back to short spurs on permanent cordons, and expect some unevenness in ripening within a cluster, which is typical of the variety.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension — Establishment and Production of Muscadine Grapes (P2290)
Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center — Muscadine Grape factsheet

common_name: Oh My! Muscadine Grape (Seedless Bronze Muscadine)

planting.note: Plant licensed nursery vines (this patented cultivar may not be propagated from cuttings) in late winter to early spring on a strong arbor or trellis; Oh My! is self-fertile and produces full-sized, tender-skinned bronze grapes that are genuinely seedless.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy overhead arbor or high-wire trellis; Oh My! is the first muscadine bred to reliably produce full-sized, seedless bronze fruit, the result of a multi-decade breeding effort by North Carolina grape breeder Jeff Bloodworth and protected under U.S. utility patent, so home gardeners should buy vines from a licensed nursery rather than propagate cuttings. The tender-skinned berries are unusually high in sugar and eat almost like a table grape, without the tough hull and swallow-or-spit seeds of a typical muscadine. Self-fertile, it needs no separate pollinator vine and ripens in early to mid-September in the Gulf South. Like other muscadines, the vine carries strong native resistance to Pierce's disease and the fungal pressures of humid summers, so it needs no spray program beyond routine winter pruning to short spurs on permanent cordons.
sources: U.S. Patent and Trademark Office — U.S. Patent 9,706,726, SSC Induction in Vitis muscadinia
Growing Produce — New Innovations on the Grow for Muscadine Grapes
